newsitem.title: FRANCE: France to plug tough immigration law loopholes.
newsitem.headline: France to plug tough immigration law loopholes.

text.p: The French cabinet approved a bill on Wednesday to revise the country's tough immigration laws, by boosting police powers to crack down on illegal immigration and making it easier for some families to get residence.

The bill aims to plug legal loopholes which have embarrassed the government particularly after police stormed a church and evicted 210 African immigrants in August, 10 of whom were staging a hunger strike in protest at their uncertain status.

Government spokesman Alain Lamassoure said the bill, presented by Interior Minister Jean-Louis Debre, struck a balance between clamping down on illegal immigration and preventing some immigrant families from being broken up.

"A lesson the government drew from the summer incidents... was that some contradictions, complexities and loopholes in the legal system needed correcting," Lamassoure said of the bill, which is due to go before parliament.
The new bill would allow authorities to grant residence permits to some foreigners who have no legal residence rights, but have a French spouse or French children.

Tough immigration laws pushed through in 1993 by former interior minister Charles Pasqua placed some immigrants in a legal no man's land because, although they could not be expelled, they were not entitled to residence.

Some immigrants have been threatened with expulsion while their children have been allowed to stay. But lawyers have successfully fought expulsion by arguing it would violate a European convention guaranteeing family integrity.

Left-wing parties and human rights groups had called on the centre-right government to review or repeal the 1993 laws which they said had been intended as a sap to Jean-Marie Le Pen's anti-immigration National Front party.
Lammassoure said President Jacques Chirac told the cabinet meeting measures were needed to cut the time it takes to get French citizenship. At present it takes five to seven years.

It doubled to 48 hours the deadline for authorities to hand over suspected illegal immigrants to a judge. It also allowed authorities to detain a suspected illegal immigrant until an appeal has been heard against a judge's decision to release him.
The bill said aliens defying expulsion orders could be face up to three months in jail. It would allow police to conduct identity checks in workplaces to crack down on illegal labour.
